title: The promotion race

card.idea: When both sides have a passed pawn, stop defending and start counting. Work out how many moves each pawn needs, remember that the side to move gets there first on a tie, and then check the one thing counting misses: whether the new queen arrives with check, or whether a king is already standing in the way.
card.habit: Activate the king and attack pawns in the endgame.

explain.text: A real race. White's a5 pawn needs three moves; Black's h4 pawn needs three moves; both kings are far from both pawns. White is to move, so White queens first. Do not spend a move on the king here — a single quiet move hands the race to Black.

Same pawns, one difference: the white king sits on h2, squarely on the h-pawn's road. Black can play h3, and then the pawn is stuck — h2 is occupied and the king simply takes it. So this is not a race at all. Count first and you will see there is nothing to fear.

Counting is the whole skill. Three moves for the pawn, and the black king on e7 is four files from the a-file — outside the pawn's square, as the last lesson showed. Whenever you are about to defend a passed pawn, check whether you can just outrun it instead.

challenges.prompt: Tap the square White's pawn is racing to.
challenges.reason: a8, three moves away. Black's pawn needs three moves to reach h1, so the side to move wins the race — and that is White.

challenges.prompt: Both pawns need three moves and it is your turn. Start running.

wrong.Kf2: A move spent on the king is a move given to the h-pawn, and now Black queens first.

challenges.reason: a6. Three moves each and you move first, so you arrive first. Any king move throws that tempo away and loses the race you were winning.

challenges.prompt: Your king already blocks the h-pawn. Get on with your own.

wrong.Kh3: Fussing over a pawn that is going nowhere. Meanwhile the black king walks into the a-pawn's square.

challenges.reason: a6 and queen. The h-pawn can reach h3 and no further, because your king stands on h2 and takes it — so there is no race to lose and no reason to hesitate.

challenges.prompt: Why is Black's h-pawn harmless in this position?
options: The white king stands on h2, directly on the pawn's road, and will capture it.
A pawn on the h-file may not promote to a queen.
Black's king is too far away to escort it.

hints.text: Look at what is sitting on the squares the pawn still has to cross.

challenges.reason: The king is in the way. A passed pawn stops being passed the moment something occupies the file in front of it, and here that something also attacks h3.

challenges.prompt: Run the race. Push, let him push, push again.
challenges.reason: Both pawns sprint and neither king can help. After a7 you are one move from a queen and Black is two — which is the margin you started with, kept intact.

challenges.prompt: Both pawns need the same number of moves. What decides a tie like this?
options: The side to move gets there first, so count from whoever's turn it is.
The pawn nearer the edge of the board promotes first.
A tie means both promote and the game is automatically drawn.

hints.text: Three moves each, but somebody has to go first.

challenges.reason: Whoever is to move. That is why a single quiet move is so expensive in a race: it does not lose you a pawn, it loses you the tie-break.

challenges.prompt: Win the race. Make a queen before Black does.
challenges.reason: Push every move and do not look back. Three pushes and you have a queen; the moment you spend a turn on the king, the count turns against you.

takeaway: Count both pawns before you defend. Equal counts go to the side to move — and a single quiet move is enough to lose the race.
